## Learning Objectives


1. Analyze a single numerical variable using the \alert{one-sample $t$-test}
2. Quantify uncertainty in the sample mean using confidence intervals
3. Compare the means of *two* numerical variables using the \alert{two-sample $t$-test}
4. Quantify uncertainty in the difference between means using confidence intervals

## Which way do Cook pines lean?

Cook pine (*Araucaria columnaris*) is endemic to New Caledonia (Southern hemisphere), but common in many parts of the world, including Hawai\`i

![From Johns *et al.* (2017): "Typical cultivated stand of *Araucaria columnaris* at the University of California, Irvine campus"](../img/johns-etal-2017-fig1.jpeg){width=40%}

## Which way do Cook pines lean?

Johns *et al.* (2017) measured axial lean of Cook pines planted all over the world. Their biological hypothesis was that Cook pines lean toward the equator.

Axial lean:

* Positive value $\rightarrow$ tree leans toward equator

* Negative value $\rightarrow$ tree leans away from equator

## The sampling distribution of the difference between sample and population mean

We want to know the sampling distribution for the difference between sample mean $\overline{Y}$ and the population mean $\mu$

$Z$-standardization gives us a standard normal sampling distribution (mean = 0, sd = 1):

$$Z = \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu}{\sigma_{\overline{Y}}}$$

BUT, we don't know the population standard error of the mean $\sigma_{\overline{Y}}$, we have to estimate from the sample $\textrm{SE}_{\overline{Y}}$.

## Student's $t$ distribution

> The difference between the sample mean and the true mean ($\overline{Y} - \mu$), divided by the estimated standard error ($\textrm{SE}_{\overline{Y}}$), has a Student's $t$-distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom.


## Student's $t$ distribution {.t}

The $t$ distribution accounts for the fact that we have to estimate both $\mu$ and $\sigma$ from the sample

$$t = \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu}{\textrm{SE}_{\overline{Y}}}$$

$t$ is like $Z$ except there is uncertainty about the sample standard error

## Student's $t$ distribution {.t}

The $t$ distribution accounts for the fact that we have to estimate both $\mu$ and $\sigma$ from the sample

$$t = \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu}{\textrm{SE}_{\overline{Y}}}$$

$t$ is like $Z$ except there is uncertainty about the sample standard error

\begin{columns}
\column{\textwidth}
  \metroset{block=fill}

  \begin{alertblock}{Pause \& Think}
  
  How would you expect the uncertainty of the estimated standard error to affect the shape of the $t$ distribution relative to the $Z$ distribution?
  
  \end{alertblock}

\end{columns}




## Student's $t$ distribution

```{r, fig.align='center', out.height="75%"}


df1 <- crossing(x = seq(-4, 4, 0.01), nesting(
  Distribution = c("t", "Z"), 
  df = c(4, Inf))) %>%
  mutate(y = dt(x, df))

ggplot(df1, aes(x, y, color = Distribution)) +
  geom_line(size = 2) +
  scale_color_discrete(labels = c(parse(text = c("italic(t)[4]")), parse(text = c("Z")))) +
  xlab(expression(italic(t)~or~italic(Z))) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 18),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 20),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 18)
  )

```

## Student's $t$ distribution

The $t$ distribution is like the standard normal ($Z$) but has longer tails that account for the fact that we estimate $\sigma$ from the sample

This matters because $P$-values are calculated by integrating the tails of the distribution. Change in the shape of the tails affect your inference!

## \alert{One-sample $t$-test}

> The \alert{one-sample $t$-test} compares the mean of a random sample for a normal population with the population mean proposed in a null hypothesis

## Null hypothesis testing

1. State null and alternative hypotheses
2. Calculate test statistic
2. Identify null distribution 
3. Calculate $P$-value
4. Decide:

    - Reject null
    - Fail to reject null


## 1. Null and alternative hypotheses

$H_0$: The true (population) mean equals $\mu_0$

$H_A$: The true (population) mean does not equal $\mu_0$

Often, $\mu_0 = 0$, like in our example:

$H_0$: The mean axial lean is 0 ($\mu = 0$)

But $\mu_0$ could be something else depending on what you're testing

## 2. The $t$ test statistic

$$t = \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu_0}{\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}}$$

## Which way do Cook pines lean?

> `-0.04, 0.00, 0.06, 0.12, 0.20`

| $\overline{Y}$     | $s$             | $s^2$            |
|:------------------:|:---------------:|:----------------:|
| `r round(ybar, 3)` | `r round(s, 3)` | `r round(s2, 3)` |

\begin{columns}
\column{\textwidth}
  \metroset{block=fill}

  \begin{alertblock}{Pause \& Think}
  
  Calculate $\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}$ and the $t$ test statistic.
  
  \end{alertblock}

\end{columns}

## Which way do Cook pines lean?

> `-0.04, 0.00, 0.06, 0.12, 0.20`

| $\overline{Y}$     | $s$             | $s^2$            |
|:------------------:|:---------------:|:----------------:|
| `r round(ybar, 3)` | `r round(s, 3)` | `r round(s2, 3)` |

\begin{columns}
\column{\textwidth}
  \metroset{block=fill}

  \begin{alertblock}{Pause \& Think}

$$\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{`r round(s, 3)`}{\sqrt{5}} = `r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)`$$

$$t = \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu_0}{\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}} = \frac{`r round(ybar, 3)` - 0}{`r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)`} = `r round(ybar/ (s/sqrt(5)), 3)`$$

  \end{alertblock}

\end{columns}

## 3. The $t$ distribution is the sampling distribution for $t$

Remember: the $t$-distribution comes from the standard normal, but with added uncertainty about the standard deviation.

We *estimate* the standard deviation, and account for its uncertainty, with a \alert{$\chi^2$ distribution}. 

Thus our $t$-distribution has degrees of freedom: $df = n - 1$

For our study, $5 - 1 = 4$ degrees of freedom

## 3. The $t$ distribution is the sampling distribution for $t$

The $t_4$ distribution looks like this:

```{r, fig.align="center", out.width="50%"}

test_stat <- ybar / (s / sqrt(5))

df <- tibble(t = seq(-4, 4, 0.01), y = dt(t, 4))

alpha <- 0.05
critical_value <- qt(
  p = alpha / 2,
  df = 4, # n = 5, df = n - 1
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

ggplot(df, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_line(size = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = test_stat, size = 2) +
  xlab(expression(italic(t)[4])) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 30),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 36)
  )

```



## 4. $P$-values

\alert{One-sample $t$-test} is usually two-sided because we would be equally surprised by a positive or negative difference from $\mu_0$

The $t$ distribution is symmetrical around 0, so we can find the area under of the curve greater/less than and our test statistic and use that same value, times -1, on the other side

```{r, fig.align="center", out.width="50%"}

ggplot(df, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, t > test_stat), fill = "tomato") +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, t < -test_stat), fill = "tomato") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(test_stat, -test_stat), color = "grey", size = 2) +
  geom_line(size = 3) +
  xlab(expression(italic(t)[4])) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 30),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 36)
  )

```

## 4. $P$-values

For a two-tailed test (most common)

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = TRUE}

P_value <- 2 * pt(
  q = 1.592,
  df = 4,
  lower.tail = FALSE
)

P_value
```

## 4. $P$-values

For a one-tailed test (less common)

```{r, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}

P_value <- pt(
  q = 1.592,
  df = 4,
  lower.tail = FALSE # test if mu > mu_0
  # lower.tail = TRUE # test if mu < mu_0
)

```

## 4. $P$-values: Even easier with the function `t.test`

```{r echo = TRUE}
y <- c(-0.04, 0.00, 0.06, 0.12, 0.20)
t.test(y)
```

## 5. Decide

Since $P = `r round(P_value, 3)`$ is greater than $\alpha = 0.05$, we fail to reject the null hypothesis.

We don't have enough evidence to conclude that Cook pines lean towards the equator from this sample




## Confidence intervals for the mean

Recall that previously we used the $2~\mathrm{SE}$ approximation

The $t$ intervals are more precise assuming the population is truly normally distributed


## 95% confidence intervals for the mean

Recall definition of confidence intervals: 95% of the time, 95% confidence intervals will include the true population mean

## 95% confidence intervals for the mean

$$-t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} < \frac{\overline{Y} - \mu}{\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}} < t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}}$$

```{r, fig.align="center", out.width="75%"}

ggplot(df, aes(t, y)) +
  geom_area(data = filter(df, t < critical_value, t > -critical_value), fill = "tomato") +

  geom_vline(xintercept = c(critical_value, -critical_value), color = "grey") +
  geom_line(size = 3) +
  geom_label(
    data = tibble(t = c(-critical_value, critical_value), y = rep(0.3, 2),
                  label = c("-italic(t)[list(0.05(2),4)]", "italic(t)[list(0.05(2),4)]")),
    mapping = aes(label = label), parse = TRUE, size = 10
  ) +
  xlab(expression(italic(t)[4])) +
  ylab("Probability density") +
  theme_cowplot() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(size = 30),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 36)
  )


```


## 95% confidence intervals for the mean {.t}

$$\overline{Y}-t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}< \mu < \overline{Y}+t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}$$

For $n = 5$, we have 4 degrees of freedom, so we calculate $t_{0.05(2),4}$

\column{\textwidth}
  \metroset{block=fill}

## 95% confidence intervals for the mean {.t}

$$\overline{Y}-t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}< \mu < \overline{Y}+t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}$$

For $n = 5$, we have 4 degrees of freedom, so we calculate $t_{0.05(2),4}$

```{r echo = TRUE}
critical_value <- qt(0.025, 4, lower.tail = FALSE)
critical_value
```

$$t_{0.05(2),4} = `r round(critical_value, 3)`$$

## 95% confidence intervals for the mean {.t}

$$\overline{Y}-t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}< \mu < \overline{Y}+t_{0.05(2),\mathit{df}} \text{SE}_{\overline{Y}}$$

For $n = 5$, we have 4 degrees of freedom, so we calculate $t_{0.05(2),4}$

```{r echo = TRUE}
critical_value <- qt(0.025, 4, lower.tail = FALSE)
critical_value
```



 
## 95% confidence intervals for the mean {.t}


$$\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}} = `r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)`$$
$$t_{0.05(2),4} = `r round(critical_value, 3)`$$


Lower 95\% CI: $`r round(ybar, 3)` - `r round(critical_value, 3)` \times `r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)` = `r round(ybar - critical_value * s/sqrt(5), 3)`$

Upper 95\% CI: $`r round(ybar, 3)` + `r round(critical_value, 3)` \times `r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)` = `r round(ybar + critical_value * s/sqrt(5), 3)`$

$$\text{SE}_{\overline{Y}} = `r round(s/sqrt(5), 3)`$$
$$t_{0.05(2),4} = `r round(critical_value, 3)`$$
